questions.stem: A post-op patient on morphine has a respiratory rate of 8 and is difficult to rouse. What should the nurse do FIRST?
options: Document the finding and reassess in 1 hour
Withhold the opioid, stimulate the patient, and support the airway
Give the next dose early to prevent breakthrough pain
questions.rationale: Respiratory depression is the most serious opioid adverse effect. Withhold the dose and contact the physician if RR is under 10. Support ABCs, then naloxone per order. [slides 24, 39]

questions.stem: What is the drug of choice to reverse opioid-induced respiratory depression?
questions.rationale: Naloxone is a pure opioid antagonist. Flumazenil reverses benzos; acetylcysteine is the acetaminophen antidote. [slide 33]

questions.stem: Naloxone is given for a suspected overdose but the patient does not improve. What does this suggest?
options: The condition may not be an opioid overdose
questions.rationale: Failure to significantly reverse the effects means the condition may not be related to opioid overdose. [slide 33]

questions.stem: 1 mg of IV hydromorphone (Dilaudid) is equivalent to how much morphine?
questions.rationale: Equianalgesia: 1 mg IV/IM hydromorphone = 7 mg morphine (about 7× stronger). [slides 22, 30]

questions.stem: Why is meperidine not recommended for long-term use?
options: Its metabolite normeperidine accumulates and can cause seizures
questions.rationale: Normeperidine is a neurotoxic metabolite that can cause seizures. [slide 17]

questions.stem: Which opioid has a prolonged half-life that has caused unintentional overdoses, and can prolong the QT interval?
questions.rationale: Methadone: long-acting synthetic mu agonist; long half-life → unintentional overdoses; prolonged QT → dysrhythmias. [slide 32]

questions.stem: Which opioid is the prototype for all opioid drugs?
questions.rationale: Morphine: naturally occurring alkaloid from the opium poppy, the prototype; Schedule I; for severe pain. [slide 29]

questions.stem: Which group of drugs has an analgesic ceiling effect?
questions.rationale: Ceiling effect: analgesia stops improving with higher doses, but side effects may increase. [slide 19]

questions.stem: Which finding suggests a possible opioid overdose?
questions.rationale: Pinpoint pupils indicate possible overdose. Classic triad: pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression, decreased LOC. [slide 24]

questions.stem: A patient on long-term opioids needs a larger dose for the same pain relief. This is:
questions.rationale: Tolerance is an expected adaptation and should not be confused with psychological dependence (addiction). [slides 26–27]

questions.stem: What is the maximum daily dose of acetaminophen for a healthy adult?
questions.rationale: 4 g/day; 2 000 mg is being considered for older adults and liver disease. Watch combination products. [slide 35]

questions.stem: What is the antidote for acetaminophen overdose, and which organ is damaged?
questions.rationale: Overdose causes hepatic necrosis; antidote is acetylcysteine. Monitor ALT/AST. [slides 36–37]

questions.stem: Which statement about acetaminophen is correct?
options: It is analgesic and antipyretic with little to no anti-inflammatory effect
It is safe in liver failure
questions.rationale: Analgesic and antipyretic, little/no anti-inflammatory effect. Contraindicated in liver dysfunction and G6PD deficiency. [slides 34, 36]

questions.stem: Which drug is an adjuvant for neuropathic pain?
questions.rationale: Neuropathic pain adjuvants: amitriptyline, gabapentin or pregabalin. [slide 18]

questions.stem: Which teaching point is correct for a patient going home on an opioid?
options: Limit fluids to prevent urinary retention
Increase fluids and fibre to prevent constipation, and change positions slowly
Take OTC sleep aids if needed
Wait until pain is severe before taking a dose
questions.rationale: Prevent constipation with fluids and fibre; change positions slowly (orthostatic hypotension); no OTCs without checking; medicate before pain is severe. [slides 39–40]

questions.stem: Which three properties do ALL NSAIDs share?
questions.rationale: All NSAIDs are analgesic, anti-inflammatory and antipyretic. Aspirin has all three PLUS platelet inhibition. [slide 3]

questions.stem: Which COX enzyme helps maintain and protect the GI mucosa?
questions.rationale: COX-1 protects the GI lining; COX-2 makes prostaglandins for inflammation. Blocking COX-1 causes GI adverse effects. [slide 7]

questions.stem: Which NSAID is the most commonly used?
questions.rationale: Ibuprofen is the most commonly used NSAID; naproxen is second. [slide 9]

questions.stem: A patient has received ketorolac (Toradol) for 6 days. What is the main concern?
options: It is only for short-term use (up to 5–7 days) and can impair the kidneys
It must be given for at least 10 days to work
questions.rationale: Ketorolac is a powerful analgesic (comparable to morphine) for short-term use only. Adverse effects include kidney impairment: monitor creatinine and BUN. [slide 8]

questions.stem: Celecoxib (Celebrex) should NOT be given to a patient with which allergy?
questions.rationale: Celecoxib, the only remaining COX-2 inhibitor, is contraindicated with a known sulpha allergy. It has little effect on platelets. [slide 11]

questions.stem: Why might misoprostol be ordered with an NSAID?
options: To prevent GI bleeding by replacing blocked prostaglandins
questions.rationale: Misoprostol is a synthetic prostaglandin E1 analogue (NOT an NSAID). It inhibits gastric acid and protects the stomach lining. [slide 12]

questions.stem: Which NSAID is better tolerated in terms of GI adverse effects?
questions.rationale: Nabumetone (an enolic acid derivative) is better tolerated for GI adverse events than some other NSAIDs. [slide 10]

questions.stem: How does aspirin prevent clots?
options: Reversibly blocks COX-2 in the liver
Irreversibly inhibits COX-1 in platelets, reducing thromboxane A2
questions.rationale: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1 → less thromboxane A2 → less platelet aggregation. Other NSAIDs lack this antiplatelet effect. [slide 14]

questions.stem: A parent wants to give aspirin to a 10-year-old with influenza. What is the risk?
questions.rationale: Reye's syndrome: life-threatening neurological deficits and liver damage, triggered by salicylates during a viral illness. No salicylates for children and teens. [slides 15, 21]

questions.stem: A patient on high-dose aspirin reports ringing in the ears. This is a sign of:
questions.rationale: Tinnitus, hearing loss, dim vision, headache, dizziness, confusion, N/V/D and hyperventilation are signs of salicylism. [slide 15]

questions.stem: When should aspirin be given to a patient having an MI?
options: At the first sign of MI, often chewable
questions.rationale: Aspirin should be given at the first sign of MI and is one of the first drugs given in the ED (often chewable) if no contraindications. [slide 13]

questions.stem: Which serious NSAID adverse effect is linked to their effect on prostaglandins in the kidney?
questions.rationale: Kidney function depends partly on prostaglandins. Risk is higher with dehydration, heart failure, liver dysfunction, diuretics or ACE inhibitors. [slides 16–17]

questions.stem: The Health Canada warning about increased CV thrombotic events (MI, stroke) applies to:
questions.rationale: All NSAIDs except aspirin share the warning. Older adults are at greater risk. [slide 18]

questions.stem: Which instruction is correct for a patient taking an NSAID?
options: Take with food, milk or an antacid, and report black or bloody stools
Crush enteric-coated tablets for faster effect
questions.rationale: NSAIDs cause GI distress, so take with food, milk or antacid. Watch for bleeding in the stool. Don't crush EC tablets. Effects may take 1 week or more. [slides 21–22]

questions.stem: Which statement about CBD (cannabidiol) is correct?
options: It is the main psychoactive ingredient that causes the 'high'
It is non-psychotropic, with anti-inflammatory, antiepileptic and antiemetic properties
It is approved as first-line therapy for pain
questions.rationale: THC is psychoactive (the 'high'). CBD is non-psychotropic with anti-inflammatory, antiepileptic, antiemetic and muscle-relaxing properties. Medical uses: adjunct for MS, cancer pain, anorexia/vomiting with chemo or AIDS. [slides 24–25]

questions.stem: Opioids relieve pain by binding to which receptors?
questions.rationale: Opioids bind mu (opiate) receptors to relieve pain. [slide 17]

questions.stem: Which pair are MILD opioid agonists?
questions.rationale: Mild: codeine, hydrocodone. Strong: morphine, hydromorphone, oxycodone, meperidine, fentanyl, methadone. [slide 17]

questions.stem: An opioid that turns off some pain receptors and blocks others, giving weaker relief, is a(n):
questions.rationale: Agonist–antagonists (partial or mixed agonists) cause a weaker pain response than full agonists. [slide 20]

questions.stem: An opioid antagonist:
options: Binds the receptor and causes strong analgesia
Binds the receptor with no response and reverses opioid effects
questions.rationale: Antagonists (nonanalgesic, competitive) bind with no response and reverse opioid effects, e.g., naloxone. [slides 20, 33]

questions.stem: Which opioid is the prototype for all opioids?
questions.rationale: Morphine: naturally occurring alkaloid from the opium poppy; Schedule I; severe pain; oral, injectable, rectal, ER forms. [slide 29]

questions.stem: Codeine is more commonly used as:
questions.rationale: Codeine: less effective, ceiling effect, more commonly an antitussive; GI disturbance; combined with acetaminophen as Tylenol #3. [slide 28]

questions.stem: Which forms of fentanyl are on the slides?
options: Injection, transdermal patch (Duragesic Mat), sublingual effervescent tablet (Fentora)
questions.rationale: Fentanyl is a synthetic Schedule I opioid for moderate to severe pain. [slide 31]

questions.stem: Which opioid provides a steady effect without intense highs and lows because it stays in the body longer?
questions.rationale: Methadone is a long-acting agonist; its prolonged half-life also causes unintentional overdoses; prolonged QT. [slide 32]

questions.stem: A patient receiving meperidine long term develops seizures. Why?
options: Accumulation of normeperidine, a neurotoxic metabolite
questions.rationale: Normeperidine accumulates and can cause seizures, so meperidine isn't recommended long term. [slide 17]

questions.stem: The order reads hydromorphone 1 mg IV. This is roughly equal to:
questions.rationale: 1 mg IV/IM hydromorphone = 7 mg morphine (7× stronger). Don't confuse hydromorphone with morphine. [slides 22, 30]

questions.stem: Which drugs have an analgesic ceiling effect?
questions.rationale: Ceiling effect: maximum analgesia is reached; higher doses add side effects, not relief. [slide 19]

questions.stem: Tolerance and physical dependence with long-term opioid use are:
options: Expected and should not be confused with addiction
questions.rationale: Both are expected with long-term treatment; addiction (psychological dependence) is compulsive use for effects other than pain relief. [slides 26–27]

questions.stem: How is opioid withdrawal prevented after chronic use?
questions.rationale: Gradual dosage reduction after chronic opioid use. [slide 27]

questions.stem: What is the MOST serious opioid adverse effect?
questions.rationale: CNS depression leading to respiratory depression is the most serious adverse effect. [slide 24]

questions.stem: Which finding suggests possible opioid overdose?
questions.rationale: Pinpoint pupils indicate possible overdose. [slide 24]

questions.stem: Opioids must be used with extreme caution in which patient?
questions.rationale: Caution: respiratory insufficiency, ↑ICP, morbid obesity/sleep apnea, paralytic ileus, pregnancy. Contraindicated in severe asthma. [slide 23]

questions.stem: Which drug combination increases the risk of respiratory depression?
questions.rationale: Opioid interactions: alcohol, antihistamines, barbiturates, benzodiazepines, promethazine, MAOIs. [slide 25]

questions.stem: A patient on morphine has a respiratory rate of 9. What does the nurse do?
options: Encourage deep breathing and give the dose
Give the dose and recheck later
Withhold the dose and contact the physician
questions.rationale: Withhold and contact the physician if VS are abnormal, especially RR less than 10 breaths/min. [slide 39]

questions.stem: When should opioids be given for best pain control?
questions.rationale: Medicate before pain becomes severe; pain is the 'fifth vital sign' (0–10 scale). [slides 38–39]

questions.stem: Which teaching point prevents a common opioid adverse effect?
options: Adequate fluid and fibre intake to prevent constipation
questions.rationale: Constipation is common and may be prevented with fluids and fibre. Also change positions slowly (orthostatic hypotension). [slide 40]

questions.stem: Ketorolac, diclofenac, indomethacin and mefenamic acid belong to which NSAID class?
questions.rationale: Acetic acid derivatives: diclofenac (Voltaren), indomethacin, sulindac, etodolac, ketorolac (Toradol), mefenamic acid (Ponstan). [slide 5]

questions.stem: Ibuprofen and naproxen belong to which NSAID class?
questions.rationale: Propionic acid derivatives: flurbiprofen, ibuprofen, ketoprofen, naproxen, oxaprozin, tiaprofenic acid. [slide 6]

questions.stem: Meloxicam, piroxicam and nabumetone are:
questions.rationale: Enolic acid derivatives; used for mild to moderate OA, RA and gouty arthritis. [slides 5, 10]

questions.stem: Mefenamic acid (Ponstan) is noted on the slides as used for:
questions.rationale: Handwritten note on the slide on slide 5: mefenamic acid → menstrual cramps.

questions.stem: Which brand name matches meloxicam?
questions.rationale: Meloxicam = Mobicox (noted 'most common' on slide 5). Voltaren = diclofenac; Naprosyn = naproxen; Celebrex = celecoxib.

questions.stem: NSAIDs relieve pain and inflammation mainly by:
options: Blocking the COX enzyme, reducing prostaglandins
questions.rationale: NSAIDs block COX, inhibiting the prostaglandin (and/or leukotriene) pathway. Prostaglandins cause pain, redness, swelling and fever. [slide 7]

questions.stem: Why do NSAIDs cause GI irritation?
options: They block COX-1, which protects the GI mucosa
questions.rationale: COX-1 maintains and protects the GI lining; NSAIDs inactivate protective prostaglandins. [slides 7, 12]

questions.stem: Which statement about aspirin's antiplatelet effect is correct?
options: It irreversibly inhibits COX-1 in platelets, reducing thromboxane A2
questions.rationale: Aspirin irreversibly inhibits platelet COX-1 → less thromboxane A2. Other NSAIDs lack this antiplatelet effect. [slide 14]

questions.stem: Which NSAID's analgesic effect is comparable to morphine?
questions.rationale: Ketorolac is used mainly for its powerful analgesic effects; short-term only (5–7 days). [slide 8]

questions.stem: Which NSAID is the second most commonly used and has fewer interactions with ACE inhibitors?
questions.rationale: Naproxen: second most common, somewhat better adverse effect profile than ibuprofen. [slide 9]

questions.stem: Which adverse effects are listed for celecoxib?
options: Headache, sinus irritation, diarrhea, dizziness, lower-extremity edema, hypertension
questions.rationale: Celecoxib AEs: headache, sinus irritation, diarrhea, fatigue, dizziness, lower-extremity edema, HTN. Little platelet effect; no sulpha allergy. [slide 11]

questions.stem: Indomethacin by the oral or rectal route can:
questions.rationale: Handwritten note on the slide: oral and rectal routes can bother the stomach. Used for RA, OA, bursitis, ankylosing spondylitis, acute gout. [slide 8]

questions.stem: What daily aspirin doses are used to prevent thrombotic events, and which is better?
questions.rationale: Daily 81 mg or 325 mg tablets; both appear equally beneficial for preventing thrombotic events. [slide 13]

questions.stem: Which finding suggests chronic salicylate intoxication?
options: Tinnitus, hearing loss, confusion and hyperventilation
questions.rationale: Salicylism: ↑HR, tinnitus, hearing loss, dim vision, headache, dizziness, confusion, N/V/D, sweating, thirst, hyperventilation, glucose changes. [slide 15]

questions.stem: Which patient should NOT receive an NSAID?
options: A patient with peptic ulcer disease
A patient with a sprained ankle
questions.rationale: Contraindications: drug allergy and bleeding risk, including peptic ulcer disease, vitamin K deficiency, rhinitis (nosebleeds). [slide 16]

questions.stem: Which patients are at highest risk of NSAID kidney toxicity?
options: Patients who are dehydrated, have heart failure or liver dysfunction, or take diuretics or ACE inhibitors
questions.rationale: Kidney function depends partly on prostaglandins; these factors increase risk. [slide 17]

questions.stem: Which drug is given to reduce NSAID-related GI bleeding?
questions.rationale: Misoprostol, a synthetic prostaglandin E1 analogue (not an NSAID), replaces blocked prostaglandins. [slides 12, 16]

questions.stem: Before starting NSAID therapy, which labs are appropriate?
options: Cardiac, kidney and liver function, CBC and platelet count
questions.rationale: Assess for GI lesions/PUD and bleeding disorders; check cardiac, kidney, liver function, CBC, platelets; take a medication history. [slide 20]

questions.stem: How long might it take to see the therapeutic effect of NSAIDs for joint pain?
questions.rationale: Explain that therapeutic effects may not be seen for 1 week or more: less swelling, pain, stiffness, tenderness. [slide 21]

questions.stem: Which teaching is correct for enteric-coated aspirin?
options: Do not crush or chew it; report any unusual bleeding such as in the stool
Stop it if you feel nauseous without telling anyone
questions.rationale: EC tablets should not be crushed or chewed. Watch for unusual bleeding (stool) and report GI pain. [slide 22]

questions.stem: Benzodiazepines are often called what?
questions.rationale: Benzos are referred to as 'pam' drugs (diazepam, lorazepam, clonazepam...). [Sed 6; Psych 7]

questions.stem: Why are nonbenzodiazepines now prescribed more often than benzos for sleep?
options: Less addictive, with favourable adverse effect profiles
questions.rationale: Nonbenzodiazepines are currently more frequently prescribed: less addictive, favourable safety. [Sed 6]

questions.stem: Benzodiazepines work by enhancing which neurotransmitter?
questions.rationale: GABA is the brain's main calming neurotransmitter (the brake pedal); benzos help it press harder. [Sed 8–9]

questions.stem: Compared with barbiturates, benzodiazepines:
options: Do not suppress REM sleep as much
questions.rationale: Benzos do not suppress REM sleep as much as barbiturates do. [Sed 8]

questions.stem: Which is NOT an indication for benzodiazepines?
questions.rationale: Indications: sedation, sleep induction, muscle relaxation, anxiety/agitation, anxiety-related depression, acute seizures, alcohol withdrawal. [Sed 7]

questions.stem: Which benzo is long acting?
questions.rationale: Long acting: clonazepam (Rivotril), diazepam (Valium), flurazepam (Dalmane). [Sed 10]

questions.stem: The slide notes say which benzo is the most common Rx?
questions.rationale: Note on slide 10: lorazepam most common Rx; alprazolam, bromazepam and lorazepam most common PRN.

questions.stem: Clonazepam's brand name and slide note?
questions.rationale: Clonazepam (Rivotril), long acting; note: often for sleep. [Sed 10]

questions.stem: Which benzo was the first clinically available?
questions.rationale: Diazepam: first benzo; anxiety, alcohol withdrawal, status epilepticus, preop sedation, muscle spasms. Avoid in hepatic dysfunction. [Sed 14; Psych 10]

questions.stem: Which benzo causes amnesia and is used for procedural sedation?
questions.rationale: Midazolam: preop and procedural sedation; amnesia, anxiolysis, sedation; IV in adults, oral liquid for children. [Sed 14]

questions.stem: Temazepam (Restoril) should be taken about how long before bed?
questions.rationale: Temazepam has a long onset; take about 1 hour before bed. It's a metabolite of diazepam. [Sed 14]

questions.stem: Which benzo can be given IV/IM for acute agitation and by continuous infusion for ventilated patients?
questions.rationale: Lorazepam: intermediate acting; IV/IM for agitation; infusion for ventilated patients; alcohol withdrawal; notes: panic attacks, stressful situations (planes). [Psych 11]

questions.stem: What is the antidote for benzodiazepine overdose?
questions.rationale: Flumazenil reverses benzos; otherwise symptomatic and supportive care. [Sed 12; Psych 8]

questions.stem: Benzo overdose rarely causes respiratory depression UNLESS:
options: Taken with other CNS depressants such as alcohol or opioids
questions.rationale: Overdose: somnolence, confusion, coma, diminished reflexes; respiratory depression rare unless combined with other CNS depressants. [Sed 12]

questions.stem: Which juice interacts with benzodiazepines?
questions.rationale: Grapefruit juice; also azole antifungals, verapamil, diltiazem, protease inhibitors, macrolides, kava, valerian. [Sed 13]

questions.stem: Benzo interactions are more likely in patients with:
questions.rationale: Interactions are more likely with renal or hepatic compromise (kidneys not excreting properly). [Psych 9]

questions.stem: Which adverse effect is listed as most common in the elderly?
questions.rationale: Adverse effects: headache, drowsiness, paradoxical excitement, dizziness (most common in elderly), cognitive impairment, 'hangover', fall hazard. [Sed 11]

questions.stem: An older adult takes a benzo at bedtime. Top priority?
options: Fall prevention: side rails/bed alarm, call light, assist with ambulation
questions.rationale: Benzos are a fall hazard for older adults; monitor for oversedation and CNS depression. [Sed 11, 25; Psych 13]

questions.stem: Which teaching is correct for a patient taking a benzo for sleep?
options: Avoid alcohol and other CNS depressants; check before OTC meds
Double the dose if you can't sleep
questions.rationale: Avoid alcohol and CNS depressants; check with the prescriber before other meds. Take hypnotics 30–60 min before bed. [Sed 24]

questions.stem: Most benzodiazepines used for sleep can cause:
questions.rationale: Most benzos cause REM rebound and a tired feeling the next day; use caution in older adults. [Sed 24]

questions.stem: What is the difference between a sedative and a hypnotic?
options: Sedatives reduce nervousness and excitability; hypnotics cause sleep and are more potent
questions.rationale: A sedative can become a hypnotic at a large enough dose: sedative-hypnotics are dose dependent. [Sed 3–5]

questions.stem: What are the three main groups of sedative-hypnotics?
questions.rationale: Barbiturates, benzodiazepines and miscellaneous drugs. [Sed 5]

questions.stem: REM interference means:
options: REM increases after stopping a drug
A drug disrupts the amount or quality of REM sleep
questions.rationale: REM interference = a drug disrupts REM. REM rebound = REM returns in excess when a REM-suppressing drug is suddenly stopped. [Sed 2]

questions.stem: Why are barbiturates rarely used today?
options: They are habit forming with a low therapeutic index
questions.rationale: Introduced in 1903; habit forming, low therapeutic index; replaced by safer benzodiazepines. [Sed 16]

questions.stem: Where do barbiturates act, and how?
questions.rationale: The reticular formation controls alertness; potentiating GABA inhibits impulses in the cerebral cortex → less anxiety, relaxation, sedation. [Sed 17]

questions.stem: Which is a barbiturate indication?
questions.rationale: Indications: sedatives, anticonvulsants, anaesthesia for surgery. [Sed 16]

questions.stem: Which hematological adverse effects can barbiturates cause?
questions.rationale: Also CV: vasodilation, hypotension; resp: respiratory depression; other: Stevens-Johnson syndrome. [Sed 18]

questions.stem: A barbiturate overdose most often leads to:
questions.rationale: Overdose → respiratory depression/arrest; CNS depression from sleep to coma and death. [Sed 19]

questions.stem: How is a barbiturate overdose treated?
options: Symptomatic and supportive: airway, ventilation/O2, fluids, alkalization, activated charcoal
questions.rationale: There's no antidote for barbiturates. [Sed 19]

questions.stem: A patient on warfarin starts a barbiturate. What may happen?
options: Reduced anticoagulant response, possible clot formation
questions.rationale: Barbiturates increase metabolism of anticoagulants → reduced response → possible clots. MAOIs prolong barbiturate effects. [Sed 20]

questions.stem: Phenobarbital is used today for:
options: Preventing tonic-clonic and febrile seizures, and neonatal hyperbilirubinemia
questions.rationale: Phenobarbital: prototypical long-acting barbiturate; rarely a sedative and no longer recommended as a hypnotic. [Sed 21]

questions.stem: Zopiclone (Imovane, Rhovane) is unique because of its:
questions.rationale: Short-acting benzo-like drug; short-term insomnia treatment for 7–10 days. [Sed 15]

questions.stem: Compared with benzodiazepine hypnotics, zolpidem (Sublinox) causes:
questions.rationale: Zolpidem: short-acting nonbenzodiazepine hypnotic with lower daytime sleepiness. [Sed 15]

questions.stem: OTC sleep aids such as Sleep-Eze and Unisom-2 contain:
questions.rationale: Doxylamine (Unisom-2), diphenhydramine (Sleep-Eze), acetaminophen/diphenhydramine (Extra Strength Tylenol Nighttime). With alcohol: respiratory depression or arrest. [Sed 22]

questions.stem: Before starting a sedative-hypnotic, which BP readings are taken?
questions.rationale: Baseline VS and I&O, including supine and erect BP; history; contraindications and interactions. [Sed 23]

questions.stem: After stopping a 3–4 week hypnotic regimen, a patient may experience:
options: Rebound insomnia for a few nights
questions.rationale: Rebound insomnia may occur for a few nights after a 3–4 week regimen is discontinued. [Sed 24]

questions.stem: Which is a therapeutic effect of a hypnotic?
options: Shorter sleep-induction time and fewer awakenings
questions.rationale: Better sleep, fewer awakenings, shorter sleep induction, few 'hangover' effects, improved well-being. [Sed 26]

questions.stem: Which safety measure is listed for patients on hypnotics?
options: Side rails up or bed alarm, call light in reach, assist with ambulation
questions.rationale: Safety: side rails/bed alarm, no smoking, assist older adults with ambulation, call light within reach. [Sed 25]

questions.stem: Which antidepressants are FIRST generation?
questions.rationale: First generation: tricyclics, tetracyclics, MAOIs. Second generation: SSRIs, SNRIs, miscellaneous. [Psych 20]

questions.stem: Where do TCAs fit in treatment today?
options: Second-line: when SSRIs fail, or as an adjunct
questions.rationale: TCAs have largely been replaced by SSRIs as first-line drugs. [Psych 21]

questions.stem: How do TCAs work?
options: Block reuptake of serotonin and norepinephrine so they build up at nerve endings
questions.rationale: Reuptake blockers: the 'email' stays in the inbox longer, so the message is read many times. [Psych 22]

questions.stem: Imipramine is used for which childhood condition?
questions.rationale: TCA indications: neuropathic pain (diabetes), insomnia, childhood enuresis (imipramine), OCD (clomipramine), sometimes anorexia. [Psych 21]

questions.stem: Amitriptyline (Elavil) is contraindicated in:
questions.rationale: Contraindications: drug allergy, pregnancy, recent MI. AEs: dry mouth, constipation, blurred vision, urinary retention, dysrhythmias, hypotension. [Psych 25]

questions.stem: Death from TCA overdose usually results from:
questions.rationale: TCA overdose is lethal; 70–80% die before reaching the hospital. No antidote: activated charcoal, alkalinize urine, manage seizures and dysrhythmias. [Psych 24]

questions.stem: Which adverse effects are listed for TCAs on slide 23?
options: Sedation, impotence, orthostatic hypotension, weight gain, 'cholinergic (think dry)'
questions.rationale: Slide 23 as written. Dry effects = dry mouth, constipation, urinary retention, blurred vision. [Psych 23, 25]

questions.stem: Which MAOI is selective and used for Parkinson's?
questions.rationale: Nonselective: phenelzine, tranylcypromine. Selective: selegiline (Parkinson's). [Psych 26]

questions.stem: What happens if a patient on an MAOI eats aged cheese or salami?
questions.rationale: Tyramine → hypertensive crisis → possible cerebral hemorrhage, stroke, coma, death. [Psych 27]

questions.stem: Which food is SAFE for a patient on an MAOI?
questions.rationale: Avoid aged cheese, smoked/pickled/aged meats and fish, yeast extracts, red wine, fava beans; limit chocolate, soy sauce, yogurt. [Psych 27]

questions.stem: In the MAOI mnemonic, what does the 'O' stand for?
options: OTC meds: cold and cough meds, NSAIDs
questions.rationale: M: Major headache (hypertension). A: Avoid tyramine. O: OTC meds. I: Increased suicide risk. [Psych 28]

questions.stem: How long is the washout when switching from an MAOI to an SSRI, TCA or SNRI?
questions.rationale: 2-week washout to prevent serotonin syndrome. [Psych 26]

questions.stem: Which is the prototypical SSRI?
questions.rationale: Fluoxetine: depression, bulimia, OCD, panic disorder, PMDD; contraindicated with concurrent MAOI. [Psych 34]

questions.stem: Match the brand: escitalopram is…
questions.rationale: Fluoxetine = Prozac, sertraline = Zoloft, paroxetine = Paxil, fluvoxamine = Luvox, citalopram = Celexa, escitalopram = Cipralex. [Psych 29]

questions.stem: Signs of 'SSRI syndrome' (too much serotonin) include:
options: Sweating, fever, rigid muscles, restlessness, tachycardia
questions.rationale: Too much serotonin in the system. [Psych 31]

questions.stem: Which antidepressant is also used to help people quit smoking?
questions.rationale: Bupropion: Zyban was the first nicotine-free Rx for nicotine dependence; also added when SSRIs cause sexual side effects. [Psych 32]

questions.stem: Duloxetine (Cymbalta) is described as 'dual action' because it treats:
questions.rationale: Depression, GAD, diabetic neuropathy, fibromyalgia, chronic back pain, OA. Watch hepatotoxicity; serotonin syndrome with SSRIs/triptans. [Psych 33]

questions.stem: Which antidepressant is sedating and used as an appetite stimulant?
questions.rationale: Mirtazapine: sedation, increased appetite, abnormal dreams, dry mouth, constipation. [Psych 35]

questions.stem: A patient started an antidepressant 1 week ago and says it isn't working. What should the nurse say?
options: It may take several weeks to see the effect; take it every day
Take it only on bad days
questions.rationale: Inform patients it may take several weeks; must be taken every day; no abrupt withdrawal. [Psych 36, 38, 53]

questions.stem: Why are antidepressant patients monitored closely in the first weeks?
questions.rationale: Monitor closely, assess suicidal tendencies, provide support; dispense small amounts. [Psych 36, 52–53]

questions.stem: Antipsychotics are mainly used to treat:
questions.rationale: Drug-induced psychoses, schizophrenia, autism; also extreme mania (with lithium), BPD, resistant depression, Tourette's, nausea, intractable hiccups. [Psych 40]

questions.stem: What is the hallmark of psychosis?
questions.rationale: Psychosis impairs mental function so the person can't do ADLs; hallmark is loss of contact with reality. [Psych 6]

questions.stem: How do antipsychotics work?
options: Block dopamine receptors in the brain, decreasing CNS dopamine
questions.rationale: Block dopamine receptors in the limbic system and basal ganglia → tranquilizing effect in psychotic patients. [Psych 41]

questions.stem: Conventional (first-generation) antipsychotics include which group?
questions.rationale: Types on slide 41: conventional/first-generation (phenothiazines), second-generation, atypical. [Psych 41]

questions.stem: Prochlorperazine is listed as an antipsychotic used as a(n):
questions.rationale: Prochlorperazine (antiemetic) is listed under antipsychotic indications. [Psych 41]

questions.stem: Atypical antipsychotics block which TWO receptors?
questions.rationale: Blocking D2 'turns down the volume'; blocking 5-HT2 lets dopamine rise where it's too low. Better balance = improved efficacy and safety. [Psych 47]

questions.stem: Which brand matches quetiapine?
questions.rationale: Clozaril, Risperdal, Zyprexa (olanzapine), Seroquel (quetiapine), Zeldox, Abilify (aripiprazole), Invega, Saphris, Latuda. [Psych 46]

questions.stem: Which brand matches aripiprazole?
questions.rationale: Aripiprazole = Abilify; lurasidone = Latuda; paliperidone = Invega; ziprasidone = Zeldox. [Psych 46]

questions.stem: Clozapine (Clozaril) causes minor or no EPS, but its key adverse effect is:
questions.rationale: Clozapine selectively blocks dopamine in the mesolimbic region; watch for blood dyscrasias. [Psych 48]

questions.stem: Risperidone (Risperdal) is noted for:
options: Causing severe EPS at any dose
Treating schizophrenia including negative symptoms, with minimal EPS at 1–6 mg/day
questions.rationale: Oral and long-acting injectable forms. [Psych 49]

questions.stem: Haloperidol (Haldol) is contraindicated in patients with:
questions.rationale: Contraindications: hypersensitivity, Parkinson's disease, large amounts of CNS depressants. [Psych 45]

questions.stem: Why is haloperidol useful for nonadherent patients with schizophrenia?
questions.rationale: Oral and IM forms; useful when patients are nonadherent. Report tremors, N/V or uncontrollable shaking. [Psych 45]

questions.stem: High fever, unstable blood pressure and myoglobinemia suggest:
questions.rationale: NMS is potentially life threatening. [Psych 43]

questions.stem: Painful muscle spasms soon after starting an antipsychotic are:
questions.rationale: EPS listed: pseudoparkinsonism-akathisia (distressing muscle restlessness) and acute dystonia (painful muscle spasms). [Psych 43]

questions.stem: Which drugs treat EPS?
questions.rationale: Benztropine (Kynesia) and trihexyphenidyl hydrochloride. [Psych 43]

questions.stem: Involuntary lip, tongue and facial movements after long-term antipsychotic use are:
questions.rationale: Tardive dyskinesia: involuntary oral/facial contractions and choreoathetosis; occurs with continuous long-term therapy. [Psych 44]

questions.stem: Which metabolic effects are listed for antipsychotics?
options: Insulin resistance, weight gain, lipid changes, cardiometabolic syndrome
questions.rationale: Also agranulocytosis and hemolytic anemia. [Psych 43–44]

questions.stem: Which teaching is correct for antipsychotics?
options: Stand up quickly to prevent dizziness
questions.rationale: Sunscreen; no antacids within 1 hour of a dose; avoid alcohol/CNS depressants; oral forms with meals; change positions slowly. [Psych 50]

questions.stem: How long should a patient wait between an antipsychotic dose and an antacid?
questions.rationale: Avoid taking antacids within 1 hour of a dose. [Psych 50]

questions.stem: Which action helps ensure a patient on psychotherapeutic drugs actually takes the oral dose?
options: Check the mouth to make sure it was swallowed
questions.rationale: Check the mouth; dispense small amounts; assess risk of harm to self and others (black box warning). [Psych 52]

questions.stem: A patient on hydromorphone has RR 9 and is hard to rouse. What should the nurse do?
options: Withhold the dose, support the airway, and notify the physician; naloxone per order
Give the next dose as scheduled
questions.rationale: Respiratory depression is the most serious opioid adverse effect. Withhold if RR is under 10 and contact the physician. Naloxone reverses opioids. [slides 24, 33, 39]

questions.stem: 1 mg IV hydromorphone (Dilaudid) equals how much morphine?
questions.rationale: Equianalgesia: 1 mg IV/IM hydromorphone = 7 mg morphine. [slides 22, 30]

questions.stem: Which opioid has a long half-life linked to unintentional overdoses and QT prolongation?
questions.rationale: Methadone: long-acting synthetic mu agonist; prolonged half-life → overdoses; prolonged QT → dysrhythmias. [slide 32]

questions.stem: Which opioid's metabolite (normeperidine) can cause seizures?
questions.rationale: Meperidine is not recommended long term because normeperidine accumulates and can cause seizures. [slide 17]

questions.stem: What is the antidote for acetaminophen overdose?
questions.rationale: Acetaminophen overdose causes hepatic necrosis; antidote is acetylcysteine. Max 4 g/day for healthy adults. [slides 35, 37]

questions.stem: Which drugs show an analgesic ceiling effect?
questions.rationale: Ceiling effect: no better pain relief at higher doses, but more side effects. [slide 19]

questions.stem: Why is aspirin avoided in children and teens with a viral illness?
questions.rationale: Reye's syndrome: progressive neurological deficits and liver damage, triggered by salicylates during viral illness. [slides 15, 21]

questions.stem: Ketorolac (Toradol) is limited to how long, and which labs are watched?
options: Up to 5–7 days; creatinine and BUN
Up to 30 days; ALT and AST
questions.rationale: Short-term use only (5–7 days) for moderate to severe pain. Adverse effects include kidney impairment: monitor creatinine and BUN. [slide 8]

questions.stem: Celecoxib (Celebrex) is contraindicated with which allergy?
questions.rationale: Celecoxib, the only remaining COX-2 inhibitor, should not be used with a sulpha allergy. Little effect on platelets. [slide 11]

questions.stem: What is misoprostol's role with NSAIDs?
options: A synthetic prostaglandin that helps prevent GI bleeding
It's an NSAID that boosts pain relief
questions.rationale: Misoprostol (NOT an NSAID) replaces prostaglandins blocked by NSAIDs: inhibits gastric acid and protects the stomach lining. [slide 12]

questions.stem: A patient on high-dose aspirin reports tinnitus. This suggests:
questions.rationale: Tinnitus and hearing loss are signs of salicylism; also N/V, confusion, hyperventilation. [slide 15]

questions.stem: Which is the most commonly used NSAID?
questions.rationale: Ibuprofen (Motrin, Advil) is most common; naproxen is second, with fewer interactions with ACE inhibitors. [slide 9]

questions.stem: What is REM rebound?
options: Increased REM when a REM-suppressing drug is suddenly stopped
Decreased REM while taking a hypnotic
questions.rationale: REM rebound occurs when a medication that suppresses REM is suddenly stopped. REM interference is when a drug disrupts REM. [slide 2]

questions.stem: Barbiturates are rarely used today mainly because they:
options: Are habit forming with a low therapeutic index
questions.rationale: Barbiturates are habit forming with a low therapeutic index; benzodiazepines are safer. [slide 16]

questions.stem: What is the treatment for a barbiturate overdose?
options: Symptomatic and supportive care (airway, ventilation, activated charcoal)
questions.rationale: There is no antidote. Maintain airway, assisted ventilation/O2, fluids, alkalization, activated charcoal. [slide 19]

questions.stem: Phenobarbital is used to:
options: Treat insomnia as a first-line hypnotic
Prevent tonic-clonic and febrile seizures and treat neonatal hyperbilirubinemia
questions.rationale: Phenobarbital is the prototypical long-acting barbiturate; no longer recommended as a hypnotic. [slide 21]

questions.stem: Zopiclone (Imovane) is used for insomnia for how long?
questions.rationale: Zopiclone is a short-acting benzodiazepine-like drug with a very short half-life, for short-term insomnia (7–10 days). [slide 15]

questions.stem: When should a hypnotic be taken?
questions.rationale: Take 30–60 minutes before bed (depends on onset). Rebound insomnia may occur for a few nights after stopping a 3–4 week regimen. [slide 24]

questions.stem: Which food/drink interacts with benzodiazepines?
questions.rationale: Grapefruit juice; also azole antifungals, verapamil, diltiazem, macrolides, alcohol and other CNS depressants. [Sed 13]

questions.stem: Which benzo is used for preop/procedural sedation and causes amnesia?
questions.rationale: Midazolam causes amnesia, anxiolysis and sedation; IV in adults, oral liquid for children. [Sed 14]

questions.stem: An older adult is started on lorazepam at night. The nurse's top priority is:
questions.rationale: Benzos are a fall hazard for older adults (dizziness, oversedation, paradoxical excitement). Bed alarm, call light, assist with ambulation. [Sed 11, 25]

questions.stem: Which is a long-acting benzodiazepine?
questions.rationale: Long-acting: clonazepam, diazepam, flurazepam. Intermediate: alprazolam, bromazepam, lorazepam, temazepam. [Sed 10]

questions.stem: How does buspirone differ from benzodiazepines?
options: It is non-sedating, non-habit forming, and taken on a schedule (not PRN)
It is given IV for agitation
questions.rationale: Buspirone takes time to work and is given on a schedule. Don't give with MAOIs; serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs. [Psych 7, 12]

questions.stem: What is the maintenance serum level for lithium?
questions.rationale: Maintenance 0.6–1.2 mmol/L; acute mania 1–1.5. Toxicity begins over 1.5–2.0. [Psych 16]

questions.stem: A patient on lithium has vomiting, tremor and confusion. What does this suggest?
questions.rationale: GI discomfort, tremor, confusion, somnolence and seizures are signs of lithium toxicity. Hold and notify. [Psych 16]

questions.stem: Why is the sodium level important with lithium?
options: Keeping sodium normal (135–145) helps maintain therapeutic lithium levels
questions.rationale: Normal sodium helps maintain therapeutic lithium levels; low sodium → lithium retained → toxicity. [Psych 16]

questions.stem: What is the most serious adverse effect of lithium?
questions.rationale: Most serious: cardiac dysrhythmia. Long-term: hypothyroidism. [Psych 17]

questions.stem: A patient on phenelzine (an MAOI) should avoid which food?
questions.rationale: Tyramine foods (aged cheese, cured meats, red wine, fava beans, yeast extracts) → hypertensive crisis. [Psych 27]

questions.stem: How long is the washout period when switching from an MAOI to an SSRI?
questions.rationale: A 2-week washout is needed due to serotonin syndrome risk. [Psych 26]

questions.stem: Which antidepressant is also used for smoking cessation?
questions.rationale: Bupropion (Zyban) was the first nicotine-free Rx for nicotine dependence; also used when SSRIs cause sexual side effects. [Psych 32]

questions.stem: TCA overdose is dangerous mainly because of:
questions.rationale: TCA overdose is lethal (70–80% die before hospital); death from seizures or dysrhythmias; no antidote. [Psych 24]

questions.stem: Amitriptyline (Elavil) is commonly used for:
questions.rationale: Oldest, most widely used TCA; commonly for insomnia and neuropathic pain. Contraindicated after recent MI and in pregnancy. [Psych 25]

questions.stem: High fever, unstable BP and myoglobinemia in a patient on an antipsychotic suggest:
questions.rationale: NMS is potentially life-threatening: high fever, unstable BP, myoglobinemia. [Psych 43]

questions.stem: Which drug treats extrapyramidal symptoms (EPS) like acute dystonia?
questions.rationale: EPS (pseudoparkinsonism-akathisia, acute dystonia) are treated with benztropine and trihexyphenidyl. [Psych 43]

questions.stem: Clozapine (Clozaril) has minor or no EPS, but its key adverse effect is:
questions.rationale: Clozapine can cause blood dyscrasias, so blood counts are monitored. [Psych 48]

questions.stem: Which nursing action is important when giving oral psychotherapeutic drugs?
options: Give a 30-day supply to improve adherence
Allow the patient to stop when feeling better
Check the mouth to make sure doses are swallowed, and dispense small amounts
questions.rationale: Check the mouth; dispense small amounts to reduce suicide risk; avoid abrupt withdrawal. [Psych 52–53]

questions.stem: Lithium is the drug of choice for:
questions.rationale: Lithium is the drug of choice for mania; thought to potentiate serotonergic neurotransmission. [Psych 16]

questions.stem: What is the target lithium level for ACUTE mania?
questions.rationale: Acute mania 1–1.5 mmol/L; maintenance 0.6–1.2 mmol/L. [Psych 16]

questions.stem: Long-term lithium therapy may cause:
questions.rationale: Long-term treatment may cause hypothyroidism. Most serious AE: cardiac dysrhythmia. [Psych 17]

questions.stem: Which lithium adverse effect involves involuntary wavelike movements of the extremities?
questions.rationale: Choreoathetosis = involuntary wavelike movements; ataxia = generalized loss of coordination. [Psych 17]

questions.stem: Buspirone should be given:
options: On a scheduled basis, not PRN
questions.rationale: Buspirone lacks sedative effect, takes time to work and is given on a schedule. [Psych 12]

questions.stem: Buspirone should NOT be given with:
questions.rationale: Do not administer with MAOIs; serotonin syndrome risk with SSRIs. [Psych 7]

questions.stem: Which is a therapeutic effect of anxiolytics?
options: Fewer anxiety and panic attacks, improved sleep and appetite
questions.rationale: Also improved alertness, cognition and mood; less fear and irritability; more interest in self and others. [Psych 13]

questions.stem: St. John's wort has severe interactions with:
questions.rationale: Also a tyramine food–drug interaction; side effects include photosensitivity. [Psych 51]

questions.stem: A patient started haloperidol yesterday and now has a sudden, painful spasm of the neck and eyes. This is:
questions.rationale: Early + painful spasm = acute dystonia (an EPS). Treated with benztropine (Kynesia). [Psych 43]

questions.stem: After 6 years on an antipsychotic, a patient has lip smacking and tongue thrusting. This is:
questions.rationale: Late (tardy) + mouth/face movements = tardive dyskinesia, from long-term therapy. [Psych 44]

questions.stem: Which drug treats acute dystonia?
questions.rationale: EPS are treated with benztropine or trihexyphenidyl. [Psych 43]

questions.stem: Haloperidol is contraindicated in Parkinson's disease because:
options: It blocks dopamine, which Parkinson's already lacks
questions.rationale: Antipsychotics block dopamine; Parkinson's is a dopamine deficiency. Also contraindicated: hypersensitivity, large amounts of CNS depressants. [Psych 41, 45]

questions.stem: Prochlorperazine is an antipsychotic used mainly as a(n):
questions.rationale: Prochlorperazine (antiemetic): for nausea. [Psych 41]

questions.stem: A patient on lithium has vomiting, a coarse tremor and confusion. What does this suggest?
questions.rationale: Signs of lithium toxicity: GI discomfort, tremor, confusion, somnolence, seizures. Hold and notify. [Psych 16]

questions.stem: Which teaching is correct for a patient on an antipsychotic?
options: Wear sunscreen and change positions slowly
Stop it when you feel better
questions.rationale: Photosensitivity → sunscreen; no antacids within 1 hour of a dose; avoid alcohol; change positions slowly. [Psych 50]

questions.stem: Which NSAID side effect is the handwritten note on the slide about indomethacin?
options: Oral and rectal routes can bother the stomach
questions.rationale: NSAIDs irritate the GI tract; respiratory depression belongs to opioids. [Pain 2, slide 8]

questions.stem: High fever, unstable BP and myoglobinemia in a patient on an antipsychotic:
questions.rationale: NMS is potentially life threatening. [Psych 43]

questions.stem: Match the antidote to benzodiazepine overdose:
questions.rationale: Opioids → naloxone. Benzos → flumazenil. Acetaminophen → acetylcysteine. Barbiturates and TCAs → no antidote.

questions.stem: Hold an opioid and call the physician if the respiratory rate is below:
questions.rationale: The slides: RR less than 10 breaths/min. [Pain 1, slide 39]

questions.stem: Maximum daily acetaminophen for a healthy adult:
questions.rationale: 4 g/day; 2 000 mg considered for older adults and liver disease. [Pain 1, slide 35]

questions.stem: Ketorolac (Toradol) is limited to:
questions.rationale: Short-term only; watch kidneys (creatinine, BUN). [Pain 2, slide 8]

questions.stem: Why no aspirin for a teen with the flu?
questions.rationale: Salicylates during viral illness can trigger Reye's syndrome. [Pain 2, slides 15, 21]

questions.stem: A patient on phenelzine eats aged cheddar. Risk?
questions.rationale: MAOI + tyramine = hypertensive crisis (major headache). [Psych 27–28]

questions.stem: Washout when switching from an MAOI to an SSRI:
questions.rationale: 2 weeks to avoid serotonin syndrome. [Psych 26]

questions.stem: Clozapine's key adverse effect to monitor:
questions.rationale: Clozapine: minor/no EPS but blood dyscrasias. [Psych 48]

questions.stem: Most serious adverse effect of lithium:
questions.rationale: Long-term: hypothyroidism. [Psych 17]

questions.stem: Hydromorphone 1 mg IV equals morphine:
questions.rationale: Equianalgesia: 1 mg hydromorphone = 7 mg morphine. [Pain 1, slides 22, 30]

questions.stem: Treatment of the common cold is:
questions.rationale: Symptomatic only, not curative; it doesn't eliminate the pathogen [P1 slide 3].

questions.stem: Health Canada recommends OTC cough and cold products NOT be given to children younger than:
questions.rationale: Under 6 years: not effective in small children [slide 4].

questions.stem: How do H1 antihistamines work?
options: They push histamine off its receptors
They compete with histamine for unoccupied H1 receptors
questions.rationale: They block unoccupied receptors but can't push off histamine already bound, so they work better at preventing than reversing effects; give them early [slide 8].

questions.stem: H2 blockers are mainly used to:
questions.rationale: H2 antagonists reduce gastric acid (peptic ulcer disease) [slide 11].

questions.stem: Which is a NON-sedating antihistamine?
questions.rationale: Non-sedating: loratadine, cetirizine, fexofenadine. Traditional (sedating): diphenhydramine, dimenhydrinate, chlorpheniramine, promethazine [slide 13].

questions.stem: Why do non-sedating antihistamines cause less drowsiness?
options: They work peripherally, with fewer CNS effects
questions.rationale: They work peripherally and have a longer duration (once-daily dosing) [slide 14].

questions.stem: The MOST common adverse effects of antihistamines are:
options: Anticholinergic (drying) effects like dry mouth and urinary retention
questions.rationale: Dry mouth, difficulty urinating, constipation, vision changes; plus drowsiness [slide 17].

questions.stem: Antihistamines should NOT be used as the sole treatment for:
questions.rationale: Not sole therapy for acute asthma; salbutamol or epinephrine treat that [slide 16].

questions.stem: Key teaching for a patient taking an antihistamine:
questions.rationale: Avoid driving/heavy machinery, alcohol and CNS depressants; take with meals; sugarless gum or candy for dry mouth [slides 19–20].

questions.stem: Which decongestant causes REBOUND congestion with use beyond several days?
questions.rationale: Topical adrenergics: prompt, potent, but cause rebound congestion with sustained use. Oral pseudoephedrine and intranasal steroids don't [slides 24, 26–27].

questions.stem: Compared with topical decongestants, oral pseudoephedrine has:
options: Delayed onset, prolonged effect, no rebound
questions.rationale: Oral: prolonged but delayed effect, less potent than topical, no rebound [slide 24].

questions.stem: How do adrenergic decongestants relieve congestion?
options: Vasoconstriction that shrinks swollen nasal tissue
questions.rationale: They constrict small blood vessels, shrinking engorged mucosa so secretions drain [slides 24–26].

questions.stem: Pseudoephedrine requires caution in a patient with:
questions.rationale: Contraindications for adrenergics: uncontrolled cardiovascular disease/HTN, acute-angle glaucoma, diabetes, hyperthyroidism, prostatitis, history of TIA/CVA [slide 28].

questions.stem: Adverse effects of oral pseudoephedrine include:
questions.rationale: Systemic adrenergic stimulation of heart, vessels and CNS [slide 30].

questions.stem: Patients taking nasal decongestants should avoid:
questions.rationale: Avoid caffeine; report fever, cough or symptoms lasting over 1 week [slide 32].

questions.stem: Combining a nasal decongestant with an MAOI can cause:
questions.rationale: MAOIs plus sympathomimetic decongestants raise BP [slide 31].

questions.stem: The main adverse effect of intranasal steroids is:
questions.rationale: Local dryness and irritation; no rebound [slide 29].

questions.stem: Antitussives are primarily used for:
questions.rationale: Antitussives stop or reduce coughing, mainly for non-productive coughs or when coughing is harmful (e.g., after hernia repair) [slide 34].

questions.stem: Dextromethorphan differs from codeine in that it:
options: Has no analgesic effect and no CNS depression
questions.rationale: Dextromethorphan suppresses the cough centre like opioids but is non-opioid, with no analgesia or CNS depression [slide 35].

questions.stem: Where do antitussives act?
options: The cough centre in the medulla
questions.rationale: Direct action on the cough centre in the medulla [slide 35].

questions.stem: Antitussives are contraindicated in a patient with:
questions.rationale: Drug allergy, opioid dependency, respiratory depression, other CNS depressants [slide 36].

questions.stem: Guaifenesin (Robitussin) is classified as:
questions.rationale: Expectorant: aids removal of mucus by thinning secretions [slide 39].

questions.stem: A patient taking an expectorant should be encouraged to:
questions.rationale: More fluids help loosen and liquefy secretions [slide 42].

questions.stem: Expectorants are used for:
questions.rationale: Productive coughs from colds, bronchitis, sinusitis, influenza, pertussis and more [slide 41].

questions.stem: What is the drug of choice for anaphylaxis?
questions.rationale: Excess histamine causes bronchoconstriction, vasodilation and a BP drop; epinephrine is the treatment [slide 7].

questions.stem: Asthma airflow obstruction is caused by all of these EXCEPT:
options: Inflammation and edema of the bronchial mucosa
questions.rationale: Alveolar ducts and alveoli stay open; airflow TO them is obstructed by bronchospasm, inflammation, edema and thick mucus [P2 slide 3].

questions.stem: Chronic bronchitis is defined as cough and sputum for at least:
options: 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years
questions.rationale: At least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years [slide 6].

questions.stem: The three classes of bronchodilators are:
questions.rationale: Beta-adrenergic agonists, anticholinergics, xanthine derivatives [slide 7].

questions.stem: Salbutamol (Ventolin) is a:
questions.rationale: Short-acting beta₂ agonist; 'rescue puffer' [slide 8].

questions.stem: Salmeterol (Serevent) must:
options: Be used alone for acute attacks
Never be used alone; always with an inhaled corticosteroid
Be taken as often as needed
questions.rationale: LABA for maintenance; never used alone; max 1 puff twice daily [slide 16].

questions.stem: Symbicort (budesonide/formoterol) combines:
questions.rationale: A LABA + glucocorticoid combo; can also be used as a reliever in moderate to severe asthma [slide 9].

questions.stem: Epinephrine (EpiPen) is classified as a:
questions.rationale: Nonselective adrenergic stimulating alpha, beta₁ and beta₂ receptors. Salbutamol = selective beta₂ [slide 10].

questions.stem: How do beta₂ agonists cause bronchodilation?
options: Activate cAMP, which relaxes airway smooth muscle
questions.rationale: Beta₂ activation → cAMP → smooth muscle relaxation → dilation [slide 11].

questions.stem: A diabetic patient starts salbutamol. What should the nurse monitor?
questions.rationale: Beta-agonists can increase blood glucose [slide 14].

questions.stem: Overusing salbutamol can cause:
options: Loss of beta₂ selectivity → tachycardia, palpitations, tremors, anxiety, nausea
questions.rationale: At high doses, beta₁ receptors are stimulated too [slide 39].

questions.stem: Ipratropium (Atrovent) works by:
options: Blocking acetylcholine receptors so bronchoconstriction is prevented
questions.rationale: ACh causes bronchoconstriction; anticholinergics block it [slide 18].

questions.stem: Ipratropium is indicated for:
questions.rationale: Prevention of COPD bronchospasm; not for acute symptoms; also reduces secretions [slide 17].

questions.stem: The most common adverse effect of anticholinergic bronchodilators is:
questions.rationale: Also urinary retention, palpitations, increased IOP [slide 19].

questions.stem: Which teaching is correct for theophylline?
options: Crush timed-release tablets for easier swallowing
Smoking increases its metabolism and can lower its levels
It's used for immediate asthma relief
questions.rationale: Smoking enhances xanthine metabolism. Don't crush timed-release. Charcoal-broiled/high-protein/low-carb foods reduce levels [slides 24–25].

questions.stem: Which is an adverse effect of xanthines like theophylline?
questions.rationale: N/V, anorexia, GERD, tachycardia, dysrhythmias, increased urination, hyperglycemia [slide 23].

questions.stem: Xanthines are contraindicated in a patient with:
questions.rationale: Contraindications: allergy, uncontrolled dysrhythmias, seizure disorders, hyperthyroidism, peptic ulcers [slide 23].

questions.stem: Xanthine derivatives cause bronchodilation by:
questions.rationale: They inhibit the enzyme that breaks down cAMP, so cAMP rises (slide 22's 'decreased' is a typo).

questions.stem: Montelukast (Singulair) is used for:
questions.rationale: LTRA for prophylaxis and long-term asthma treatment; not for acute attacks; safe from age 2 [slide 27].

questions.stem: Teaching for montelukast:
options: Take every night, even when symptoms improve
questions.rationale: Every night on a continuous schedule; improvement in about 1 week [slides 27, 30].

questions.stem: What should be monitored with leukotriene receptor antagonists?
questions.rationale: Both montelukast and zafirlukast may cause liver dysfunction [slides 29–30].

questions.stem: Leukotrienes cause:
questions.rationale: LTRAs block them, preventing these effects [slide 28].

questions.stem: Inhaled corticosteroids like fluticasone are used for:
questions.rationale: Not sole therapy for acute attacks; full effect can take weeks [slides 31–33].

questions.stem: The most common adverse effect of inhaled corticosteroids is:
questions.rationale: Also pharyngeal irritation, cough, dry mouth; systemic effects are rare [slide 33].

questions.stem: A patient uses salbutamol and fluticasone. Correct order?
options: Salbutamol first, wait several minutes, then fluticasone
questions.rationale: Bronchodilator first opens airways so the steroid reaches deeper [slide 40].

questions.stem: Systemic corticosteroids combined with furosemide raise the risk of:
questions.rationale: Greater risk of hypokalemia with diuretics; steroids may also raise glucose [slide 34].

questions.stem: Oral corticosteroids for an asthma exacerbation are usually limited to:
options: About 5 days or a tapering dose
questions.rationale: Oral steroids usually limited to 5 days or a taper [slide 32].

questions.stem: Roflumilast (Daxas) is a:
questions.rationale: Prevents COPD exacerbations; adverse effects include weight loss and psychiatric symptoms [slide 35].

questions.stem: Omalizumab (Xolair) requires close monitoring for:
questions.rationale: Monoclonal antibody binding IgE, given by injection; potential for anaphylaxis [slide 36].

questions.stem: Normal respiratory rate the nurse expects on assessment before respiratory drugs:
questions.rationale: Respirations 12–20/min, plus skin colour, vital signs, SpO₂, sputum, allergies, history, other meds [slide 38].

questions.stem: A patient has trouble coordinating breathing with their inhaler. The nurse should:
questions.rationale: Provide a spacer; demonstrate and get a return demonstration [slide 41].

questions.stem: Which is NOT a function of the skin?
options: Provides a site for drug absorption
questions.rationale: Skin functions: protective barrier, senses temperature/pressure/pain, regulates temperature, excretes fluid and electrolytes, stores fat, synthesizes vitamin D, site for drug absorption [slide 3].

questions.stem: The two layers of the skin are the:
questions.rationale: The skin, the body's largest organ, has two layers: dermis and epidermis [slide 2].

questions.stem: Which area is commonly affected by psoriasis?
questions.rationale: Commonly affected: nails, genitals, scalp and lower back [slide 4].

questions.stem: Which description matches psoriasis lesions?
options: Thick, reddened skin covered in silvery scales
questions.rationale: Psoriasis: thick, reddened skin covered in silvery scales [slide 4]. Pale, raised, itchy bumps describe urticaria.

questions.stem: Topical corticosteroids have all of these actions EXCEPT:
questions.rationale: Their actions are anti-inflammatory, antipruritic and vasoconstrictive. They don't kill bacteria; they can actually allow bacterial overgrowth [slides 6, 8].

questions.stem: Which type of corticosteroid is used specifically for psoriasis?
questions.rationale: Fluorinated corticosteroids are used for psoriasis. 1% hydrocortisone is the low-potency OTC option [slide 6].

questions.stem: Which topical corticosteroid is available over the counter?
questions.rationale: 1% hydrocortisone is available OTC [slide 6].

questions.stem: A patient applies a topical steroid to their scalp for months. Which adverse effect is especially linked to scalp use?
questions.rationale: Alopecia, particularly when used on the scalp. Also: acne, contact dermatitis, skin fragility, hypopigmentation, burning, dryness, itch [slide 7].

questions.stem: What interaction can occur with topical corticosteroids?
options: Toxicity when oral and topical steroids are used together
Reduced effect when taken with food
questions.rationale: Toxicity can occur when oral and topical use are combined [slide 8].

questions.stem: Which patients have higher systemic absorption of topical medications?
options: Very young and very old patients
questions.rationale: Systemic absorption is higher in very young and very old patients because their skin may be more permeable [slide 14]. This is also why children get less potent steroids.

questions.stem: When must the nurse wear gloves with methotrexate?
options: When handling it in any form
Gloves are not needed for oral tablets
questions.rationale: Wear gloves when handling methotrexate in any form, and when applying topical medications [slide 15].

questions.stem: Which are adverse effects of methotrexate?
questions.rationale: Methotrexate adverse effects: headache, glossitis, gingivitis, mild leukopenia, nausea [slide 13].

questions.stem: A patient on methotrexate asks about herbal supplements. Which should they avoid?
questions.rationale: Methotrexate should not be taken with echinacea. Also use caution with live immunizations [slide 13].

questions.stem: Which routes is methotrexate available in?
questions.rationale: Methotrexate is available in IM, IV and PO preparations [slide 12].

questions.stem: When are systemic antipsoriatic drugs (biologics, methotrexate) used?
options: When topical corticosteroid therapy has not been successful
questions.rationale: Systemic antipsoriatics are used when topical corticosteroid therapy isn't successful [slide 10].

questions.stem: Biologics are also referred to as:
questions.rationale: Biologics are biological response modifiers: they alter the body's response to autoimmune, inflammatory, infectious diseases and cancer [slide 10].

questions.stem: How does lidocaine produce local anesthesia?
options: By inhibiting the transport of sodium ions across neuronal membranes
questions.rationale: Lidocaine blocks sodium transport across nerve membranes, numbing skin receptor nerve endings [slide 18].

questions.stem: What is the half-life of topical lidocaine?
questions.rationale: Short half-life: 1.5–2 hours [slide 18].

questions.stem: A patient has severe sunburn. Besides the skin, what should the nurse assess for?
questions.rationale: With severe sunburn, assess for weakness, fever, chills and shock [slide 19].

questions.stem: Besides lidocaine, which other topical anesthetic is listed for sunburn?
questions.rationale: Topical anesthetics for sunburn: benzocaine and lidocaine [slide 17].

questions.stem: Which topical form penetrates the MOST?
questions.rationale: Ointments penetrate most (greasy, stays on longest), then gels, creams and lotions [slide 7].

questions.stem: Topical corticosteroids can allow bacteria and fungi to grow on the skin because they:
questions.rationale: Local immunosuppression lets bacteria and fungi overgrow [slide 8]. Steroids are vasoconstrictive.

questions.stem: Which is a biologic used for psoriasis?
questions.rationale: Biologics: etanercept, adalimumab, ustekinumab (-cept, -mab). Methotrexate = antimetabolite; betamethasone = topical steroid [slide 10].

questions.stem: A patient on methotrexate wants ibuprofen for a headache. The nurse's main concern is:
questions.rationale: NSAIDs and ASA with methotrexate can cause toxicity [slide 13].

questions.stem: After months of heavy use, a steroid cream “doesn't work as well as it used to.” This is:
questions.rationale: Tachyphylaxis: the drug weakens with long-term use or overuse [slide 8].

questions.stem: Why isn't phototherapy combined with immunosuppressants?
questions.rationale: Phototherapy plus immunosuppression raises skin cancer risk [slide 5].

questions.stem: Which is true of topical lidocaine for sunburn?
options: Apply it generously to open blisters
Use extreme caution with complex burns because of rapid systemic absorption
It works by constricting blood vessels
questions.rationale: Not on open sores; half-life 1.5–2 h; rapid systemic absorption through complex burns [slide 18].
